title: When More Sampling Hurts: The Modal Ceiling and Correlation Ceiling of Test-Time Scaling
hook: Sample a reasoning model dozens of times and coverage keeps climbing — but picking the right answer from the pile plateaus fast, and extra samples past that point can backfire.
key_points: Test-time scaling raises 'coverage' (odds some sample is correct), but a deployed system must pick just one — that's 'selection', and it caps far below coverage.
The gap between climbing coverage and stalled selection is the 'identifiability gap': correct answers the model can produce but not reliably pick.
Selection saturates within a few dozen samples (the 'modal ceiling'); predicting a benchmark score saturates even sooner (the 'correlation ceiling').
Past the ceiling, extra samples add cost and can make the model more confidently wrong, not just flat.
Reduces the cutoff to one diagnostic number, the 'effective number of samples', readable from any sampling run already collected.
content_html: Test-time scaling — sampling a reasoning model many times and picking the best answer — looks like it keeps paying off: draw enough samples and a correct answer turns up somewhere almost every time. This paper asks a sharper question: can you actually pick that correct answer, and for how long does drawing more samples help?
extra_html:
Two different ceilings

Coverage — the fraction of problems where at least one sample is correct — climbs steadily with more draws, which is why test-time scaling looks like free progress. But a deployed system must commit to one answer without knowing which sample is right; that's selection, and it saturates far below coverage. The authors call the difference the "identifiability gap" — correct answers the model generates but a selection rule can't reliably surface. For picking a single answer (e.g. majority vote), performance flattens within a few dozen samples, the "modal ceiling." For predicting a benchmark score, it flattens even sooner, the "correlation ceiling."

Why it matters

Past either ceiling, extra samples aren't just wasted compute — the paper shows they can nudge the model into confidently converging on a wrong majority answer, making performance worse, not just flat. The authors distill the cutoff into one practical number, the "effective number of samples," that can be read off any sampling run already collected, giving practitioners a concrete stopping point instead of sampling on faith.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'identifiability gap' in this paper's terms?
flashcards.back_html: The gap between coverage (the fraction of problems where at least one sample is correct) and selection (how often you can actually pick the correct sample) — correct answers the model produces but can't reliably surface.

flashcards.prompt: What happens if you keep sampling well past the 'modal ceiling'?

choices.text: Extra samples add cost and can make the model more confidently wrong, not just plateau
Coverage and selection both keep improving indefinitely
Selection improves while coverage stays flat

flashcards.explanation_html: Selection saturates within a few dozen samples; drawing more past that point can push the model toward a confident but incorrect majority answer.

flashcards.prompt: Why does coverage climbing with more samples not mean the deployed system is getting better?
flashcards.back_html: A deployed system must commit to one answer without knowing which sample is correct. Coverage measures whether a correct answer exists somewhere in the batch; selection measures whether you can pick it, and selection caps much sooner.
